content: 1. Children living with HIV were not included in trials 242-12-232 and 233. The observed increase in pharmacokinetic parameters is not clinically significant and does not require dose adjustments. Delamanid, a weak CYP3A4 inducer, does not affect the plasma levels of antiretroviral drugs such as tenofovir, lopinavir/ritonavir, or efavirenz. No drug interaction studies have been conducted with delamanid and integrase inhibitors, but based on metabolic pathways, the risk of metabolic drug interactions is expected to be low. Therefore, delamanid can be safely administered to children living with HIV (CLHIV) with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) on antiretroviral therapy (ART) without dose adjustments. 2. Delamanid has been used in adults and adolescents since 2014, in children aged 6 years and older since 2016, and in children aged 3 years and older since 2019. The considerations for its use in children under 3 years of age are an extension of those already in place. Key considerations for this age group include dosing based on the availability of the 25 mg dispersible formulation and monitoring for neuropsychiatric side effects. 3. In clinical trials, delamanid was administered to children aged 3–5 years using a 25 mg dispersible tablet. Altering the 50 mg adult tablet (e.g., splitting, crushing, or dissolving) may affect its bioavailability. Additionally, the adult tablet is prone to shattering when split and has a bitter taste, making it unpalatable. The tablets are also sensitive to oxidation and heat, which can lead to reduced active compound delivery and the formation of oxidation by-products if pill fragments are stored for later use. 4. The child-friendly 25 mg dispersible tablet formulation of delamanid has been included in the 8th WHO Essential Medicines List for Children (EMLc) since October 2021, approved by the European Medicines Agency in September 2021, and made available through the Stop TB Partnership Global Drug Facility (GDF) since October 2021. In study 242-12-233, children aged 0–2 years were given a 5 mg pediatric dispersible formulation, which is not expected to be commercialized. No direct bioequivalence comparison has been made between the 5 mg pediatric formulation and the 50 mg adult tablet, and they are not interchangeable. 5. Dosing guidance for delamanid in children under 3 years of age is provided in the operational handbook, based on expert consultation. This guidance considers the availability of the 25 mg dispersible formulation. In trials, delamanid bioavailability was optimized by administering it with a high-fat meal, emphasizing the importance of food during administration. In neonates, frequent feedings align well with the need for higher-fat content during administration. 6. Guidance on constructing optimal treatment regimens for children with MDR/RR-TB who are not eligible for shorter, all-oral regimens is provided in the operational handbook. Shortening the total treatment duration to less than 18 months may be considered for children without extensive disease. Extensive TB disease refers to bilateral cavitary disease or extensive parenchymal damage on chest X-ray, while severe extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) includes miliary TB or tuberculous meningitis (TBM) in adolescents and adults over 15 years of age. In children under 15 years, extrapulmonary forms other than lymphadenopathy are considered severe. 7. Concurrent use of delamanid and bedaquiline, as well as delamanid use beyond six months, has been evaluated. Evidence from a 2019 GDG meeting did not allow conclusions on the effectiveness of concurrent use but suggested no additional safety concerns. Therefore, delamanid and bedaquiline may be used in patients with MDR/RR-TB who have limited treatment options, such as those with extensive drug resistance or intolerance to other second-line TB medications. Safety monitoring, including ECG and electrolyte monitoring, is essential for these patients. 8. The available evidence for delamanid use is limited to the on-label six-month duration alongside other medicines in a longer regimen. Prolongation beyond six months can be considered on a case-by-case basis. Monitoring for neuropsychiatric effects, including hallucinations, is critical, especially in children receiving other medications with known neuropsychiatric effects, such as cycloserine. Active TB drug safety monitoring and management systems must be in place to detect, manage, and report suspected or confirmed drug toxicities promptly. 9. Recording and reporting details on diagnosis, treatment regimens, clinical monitoring, and outcomes in children and adolescents with MDR/RR-TB are crucial for monitoring the implementation of new regimens and improving case finding. Data from national programs on delamanid use in children of all ages are essential to expand the evidence base. 10. WHO guidelines recommend that children with pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis in low HIV and isoniazid resistance settings, and who are HIV-negative, be treated with a three-drug regimen (HRZ) for two months followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for four months. Children with severe pulmonary disease should receive a four-drug regimen (HRZE) for two months followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for four months. Infants aged 0–3 months with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB should be promptly treated with a six-month regimen (2HRZ(E)/4HR), with dose adjustments as needed. 11. Children with suspected or confirmed osteoarticular TB should be treated with a four-drug regimen (HRZE) for two months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for ten months, totaling 12 months of treatment. Streptomycin should not be used as part of first-line treatment regimens for children with pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis. 12. For patients with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, daily dosing is recommended over thrice-weekly dosing during both the intensive and continuation phases of therapy. Fixed-dose combination (FDC) tablets are preferred over separate drug formulations for treating drug-susceptible TB. 13. In patients with rifampicin-susceptible, isoniazid-resistant TB, a six-month regimen of rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin is recommended. Streptomycin or other injectable agents should not be added to the treatment regimen. 14. A shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen of 9–12 months is recommended for eligible patients with MDR/RR-TB who have not been exposed to second-line TB medicines for more than one month and in whom fluoroquinolone resistance has been excluded. 15. For longer regimens in MDR/RR-TB, all three Group A agents and at least one Group B agent should be included to ensure treatment starts with at least four effective TB agents. If only one or two Group A agents are used, both Group B agents should be included. Group C agents may be added if the regimen cannot be composed with agents from Groups A and B alone. Kanamycin and capreomycin should not be included in longer regimens. Levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, linezolid, clofazimine, and cycloserine or terizidone may be included in longer regimens. Ethambutol and pyrazinamide may also be included, while amikacin may be used in patients aged 18 years or older when susceptibility is demonstrated, and adequate monitoring for adverse reactions is ensured.
